title: Míriel of the Emerald Veil
type: NPC · Emerald Veil scholar, cultural organizer and political speaker
dek: A civic organizer and arcane researcher who welcomes Olokun, opens a working Void passage and brings strong loyalties into the struggle over Aria’s legacy.

facts.Age account: Says she has lived roughly three hundred years; birth date unverified
facts.Established work: Olokun’s admission · cultural tour · coordinated portal and Gates
facts.Research limit: Passage achieved; complete Void healing not established
facts.Political record: Candidate who also favors Magnus; formal later position unresolved

body:
Míriel makes knowledge useful through people: a welcome, a badge, an introduction, a carefully chosen tour or a team of archmages. She helps outsiders enter Zarathian life and prepares a passage into the Void. When their choices threaten the people and institutions she values, her hospitality becomes much harder to separate from judgment and ambition.

Information, hospitality and a name of her own

Míriel introduces the Emerald Veil through food, clothing, money, celebrations and libraries. The society she wants the newcomers to see depends on many people doing small things well. Courts and powerful magic are only part of that work.

She asks to be called Míriel rather than addressed through titles. In July she playfully offers grand descriptions of herself as a keeper of secrets and uncoverer of things, then returns to her name. The flourish is social self-presentation, not proof that she knows every secret.

Her welcome has expectations. She praises tact and patience, offers introductions and wants guests to understand the culture that receives them. She can be charming without being indifferent to what a visitor believes or how they behave.

Knowledge as a bond between people

In her early conversation with Olokun, Míriel asks what draws him to the council. She values diplomacy, useful contributions and the work of helping a household find its place. Her account of the Veil favors collaboration and personal relationships before the simple purchase of whatever someone needs.

She welcomes him as a member and gives him a badge, explaining the basic libraries, research facilities and help it can open to him. Greater access still requires trust. The encounter establishes this admission; it does not make every later visitor a member or open every collection to everyone.

Asked about her life, she says she has lived roughly three hundred years and credits the Verdant Circle with extending lives. This is her account of her age and local practice, not an independently recovered birth date.

She also asks Olokun to write the history of the Gate through which he arrived. She admits she does not know its workings. His experience matters to her precisely because it can supply knowledge her own institutions lack.

Research with boundaries

By the Month of Cala, Year 2, Míriel says researchers have begun finding ways to cross the Veil and perhaps heal it. She distinguishes the Gate spell from ordinary Void travel, yet again says she knows nothing of the particular Gate the company used.

She describes experiments with powerful illusions and insists that they must understand what they have done before pushing further. The reported effects belong to her research account. A hope of healing the Void is not a completed restoration, and one spell’s behavior does not settle all magic in every part of it.

That caution coexists with ambition. She is willing to pursue work that could change the reach of her society, but the later expedition will show how far opening a passage remains from understanding everything beyond it.

Who is believed, and what a tour can show

After the confrontation over Aria’s conduct, Míriel rebukes Olokun for challenging a beloved figure publicly without allies and overwhelming evidence. She says the Veil believes Aria. Her confidence shows the force of reputation inside the institution; it does not resolve the incompatible accounts of the battle.

She nevertheless praises Scribonia’s quiet discernment and says she is assembling an investigation. That is a stated plan, not a completed report. Her demand for careful evidence remains beside the unequal credibility she gives the people offering it.

At the cultural visit later that month, a different information failure irritates her. Olokun asked for a tour, but some guests now want faction admission. She brought guides for one purpose and would have chosen differently for the other.

She explains factions as institutions supporting people with shared strengths, then sends the visitors into the life of the island. On their return she asks them to share what they learned. She wants them to understand workers and ordinary relationships, not only the courts and colleges a grander tour might display.

Opening a way without knowing every destination

On 5, Month of Death, Míriel arrives inkstained and singed, smiling over a portal her team has opened after years of work. The expedition actually passes through the opening; this is more than a proposal for future travel.

She is much less certain about the object they seek. Its existence is inferred from disturbances, its form unknown, and its recovery only a possibility. Aria wants the theory tested. Míriel gives the party sending stones, arranges magical help and promises support for the passage from their side. She warns that they do not know how magic behaves in the Sea.

At the later war council she says the Veil’s mightiest magi can open great Gates to a known destination, but admits they do not know where the wider war is being fought. Her statement that they have never traveled the Void sits beside the earlier experiment: a working portal and an expedition have not given her people comprehensive routes or mastery of travel.

In the Month of the Wyrm, she still cannot identify which of three possible battlefields holds the present fighting. She is eager to learn unfamiliar magic, disappointed when an apparent discovery proves a misunderstanding, and finally orders the archmages to open Gates for the legions. Her authority is visible in coordinated work without supplying a complete formal rank.

After Aria: loyalty, grief and ambition

Aria’s death turns Míriel’s questioning toward blame. She asks for Magnus’s account, challenges the claim that Scribonia is dead and fears someone has escaped justice. When Magnus offers to pay, she distinguishes his attempt to defend his liege from the responsibility she attributes to the outsiders.

She proposes exile for everyone except Magnus. Olokun’s service does not persuade her to swallow the loss. This is an angry political proposal, not the final judgment later delivered by Bowene.

At the leadership gathering she admits that others see her as ambitious and jealous of Aria. She presents her own candidacy, yet also praises Magnus as a returned hero around whom the people can unite. The narrator separately confirms that she wants him to win. Her affection for arcane work and subtle words does not make her a neutral observer of succession.

The later memorial exposes another side of her social skill. The narrator identifies her display of crying there as false; after the divine restoration she glowers and anticipates pressing for banishment. That depiction belongs to this occasion. It should not silently turn every earlier expression of loss into a performance, or settle all the motives behind her support for Magnus.

The open history

Míriel is a cultural organizer, recruiter, researcher and political actor. Her formal rank, the full outcome of the inquiry she proposes, the completion of the hoped-for repair and her later personal position remain unresolved. She is distinct from both Captain Miriel and Mirae the librarian.

Her ability to secure cooperation and move knowledge is real. So are the limits she admits and the loyalties that shape whose evidence she will accept. Keeping those together leaves room for an accomplished person whose judgment can still serve her institution and her ambition.
